doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Why traditional jazz is overlooked
summary: Armstrong, Bix and old recordings, and how the Miles and Coltrane era drew attention away.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: It is. And I don’t want to spout it or anything but all these guys were part of musical history, for jazz history, which I don’t know, is kind of — it seems to be not ignored, but not as many people know about that part of jazz as when Miles and Coltrane were coming through at the same time. Everybody’s attention kind of went that way.
Yeah. As if that’s where things really started.

Right. Well if you go back before then it was the Dixieland guys and it was Louis Armstrong. And all those guys I worked with. We’d talk about music and different things and invariably someone would say Louis was the guy. He made it possible for everyone else. If Bix hadn’t died, where would his career have gone? How influential would he have been to maybe hear him on a more modern recording than some of that old stuff — which is wonderful stuff with Frankie Trumbauer and Chauncey Morehouse on drums. But it was old style recording.
Right. It’s kind of a shame because people listen to it and because of the sound of it it’s easy to sort of dismiss.
